Cache-Control: no-cache Must revalidate with the server before using (NOT "no cache") Cache-Control: no-store Absolutely do not store — for sensitive data. ETag + If-None-Match Content fingerprinting; server returns 304 Not Modified if unchanged → saves bandwidth. stale-while-revalidate Use the old version immediately, update silently — fast + gradually new Classic caching strategy Files with content hashes (e.g., app.a3f9.js) are cached immutably for 1 year because changing content changes the filename. The index.html file uses no-cache (always revalidate) so users receive the latest version. This is the foundation of safe deployment. CORS — why is the request blocked? Preflight request (OPTIONS) for "non-simple" requests CORS is a browser mechanism. CORS does not protect the server (requests still reach the server). It protects the user: the browser blocks JavaScript from reading responses from a different origin unless the server allows it. Therefore, CORS errors must be fixed on the server (by adding headers), not on the client. Trick question "Does no-cache mean no caching?" → No! no-cache = still stores but must revalidate (ETag) before using. "Don't store anything" is no-store. Confusing these two is a very common mistake. A CORS error appears in the console. Where is the correct place to fix it? Fix client-side JavaScript code to "bypass" CORS Configure the server to return the correct Access-Control-Allow-Origin header (or use a proxy). Close the browser. Switch to using localStorage. CORS is enforced by the browser based on headers from the server. The client cannot "disable" it. The server must allow the origin, or the request must go through a same-origin proxy.

handbookTitle: Designing a Frontend System from A to Z
text: Design System & Component Library As the product and team grow, UI consistency becomes a technical challenge. A design system serves as the "single source of truth," enabling dozens of developers to create consistent interfaces without stepping on each other's toes. The layers of a Design System. From token to product Design Tokens — the heart of theming. CSS /* Token semantic points to the original token → changing the theme is easy. */ :root { --blue-500: #3b82f6; /* primitive */ --color-primary: var(--blue-500); /* semantic */ } [data-theme="dark"] { --color-primary: var(--blue-300); } /* The component only uses semantic tokens, no hardcoded colors. */ .btn { background: var(--color-primary); } Versioning & Breaking Changes Component libraries should use semantic versioning. Changing a required prop constitutes a major version. Provide codemods for automatic migration, and issue deprecation warnings at least one version before removal. This maintains trust with the teams using the library. Notable trade-off "Flexible" components (many props) vs. "opinionated" components (fewer choices, high consistency). Good libraries often use compound components and slots to achieve both flexibility and consistency, rather than cramming in 30 boolean props. Why should "semantic tokens" (--color-primary) be separated from "primitive tokens" (--blue-500)? To make the CSS file smaller To change the theme/brand by simply pointing to a different semantic token, without modifying individual components. Because the browser requires it. To avoid using CSS variables The component only references semantic tokens. When switching themes (light/dark, brand change), you simply point the semantic tokens to different primitive tokens, and all components update accordingly.

handbookTitle: Designing a Frontend System from A to Z
text: Testing Strategy for Frontend Tests are not about achieving 100% coverage, but about having confidence to refactor and deploy. The core question: what to test, at which layer, to catch the most bugs with the lowest maintenance cost. Testing Pyramid (and the variant "Trophy") Distribute tests by layer What type of tests catch which bugs? Type What to test Popular tools Unit Pure function, util, reducer, custom hook Jest, Vitest Component / Integration Component renders correctly, user interaction, callback invocation React Testing Library E2E Complete flow: login → purchase → payment Playwright, Cypress Visual regression Does the UI break visually? Chromatic, Percy The philosophy of Testing Library "Test like how users interact" — find elements by role/label/text instead of class or internal test-id. Such tests are less brittle during refactoring and catch real bugs. Avoid testing implementation details (internal state, function names). Trap: flaky tests E2E tests become "flaky" due to timing issues (waiting for animations, network). Mitigation: wait for conditions (await expect(...).toBeVisible()) instead of sleep(2000), mock network when needed, and isolate tests (no dependency on execution order). According to the philosophy of React Testing Library, which element-finding method is most recommended? Through CSS classes like `.btn-primary` Through the component's internal state Through the role/label/text that the user can see Based on the DOM order (the 3rd element) RTL encourages querying based on what users perceive (role, label, text), making tests resilient to refactoring and reflecting real user experience. Internal class/state details are implementation specifics.

handbookTitle: Designing a Frontend System from A to Z
text: Monitoring and Observability "You cannot improve what you don't measure." After deployment, how do you know if real users encounter errors or if the page is slow? This is what distinguishes junior from senior engineers. Three pillars to monitor. Error Tracking Catch JS runtime errors, promise rejections, and API errors. Group them by category, include stack trace and breadcrumbs. Tools: Sentry, Rollbar. RUM — Real User Monitoring Measure Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS) from real users, segmented by device/network/region. This differs from lab tests (Lighthouse). Analytics & Funnel At which step did the user drop off, and which feature was used? Connect performance to user behavior and revenue. Performance Budget — set limits to avoid "drifting." JSON // Warn/block the build if it exceeds the threshold. { "budgets": [ { "resourceType": "script", "maximumError": "170kb" }, { "metric": "LCP", "maximumWarning": "2500ms" } ] } Lab data vs Field data Lab (Lighthouse) = simulated environment, stable, good for debugging. Field/RUM = real users, many device/network variations — these are the numbers that matter for SEO (Google uses CrUX). Must look at both. Source maps for production Upload private source maps (not public) to Sentry so that stack traces from minified code become readable. Do not deploy source maps publicly to avoid source code exposure. Google uses field data from the Chrome User Experience Report (CrUX) to evaluate Core Web Vitals for search rankings. Lighthouse scores run on your machine. Real user field data (CrUX / RUM) Number of lines of code on the page Number of requests Google uses the Chrome User Experience Report (CrUX) — field data from real Chrome users. Lighthouse provides lab data, useful for debugging but not directly used for ranking.

handbookTitle: Designing a Frontend System from A to Z
text: Build, Bundling & Deploy The code you write doesn't run directly in the browser. Understanding bundlers helps you reduce bundle size, improve load speed, and deploy safely with feature flags and rollback. What does a bundler do? Technique Effect Tree-shaking Remove dead code — requires ES modules for static analysis. Code splitting Split bundles by route/component, load on demand (dynamic import()). Minification Minify variable names, remove whitespace, dead code Content hashing File name with hash (app.a3f9.js) → permanent cache, content change = name change Module Federation Share the runtime module between apps (micro-frontend platform). CI/CD Pipeline & Deployment Strategy From commit to production safely Feature flags = decoupling deployment from release Deploy code to production but disable the feature behind a flag. Gradually enable it from 1% → 50% → 100%. If an error occurs, turn off the flag immediately (no need to rollback the deployment). Also used for A/B testing. A valuable question How to deploy without breaking the experience for users on an old tab? → Use versioned assets with content hashes, keep old files for a period of time, and handle "chunk load failed" errors by reloading the page when a new version is detected. The main benefit of feature flags compared to using deploy/rollback is that they allow you to toggle features on or off at runtime without redeploying, enabling safer, more granular control over releases, faster rollback, and easier A/B testing or gradual rollouts. Make the bundle smaller. Separate code deployment from feature activation — enable/disable instantly without redeploying. Automatically write tests. Completely replace CI/CD Feature flags allow code to be in production while the feature remains disabled; they enable gradual activation and immediate deactivation upon errors without requiring deployment or rollback. Ideal for gradual rollouts and A/B testing.

handbookTitle: Designing a Frontend System from A to Z
sectionTitle: Bundler comparison: Webpack · Vite · esbuild · Rollup
text: Bundler comparison: Webpack · Vite · esbuild · Rollup Each build tool is created to solve a different problem. Understanding them helps you choose the right tool and explains why Vite is "lightning fast" during development. Overview comparison Tool Strong points Technical specifications Webpack Complex app, massive loader/plugin ecosystem Bundle everything; extensive configuration; module federation Vite Extremely fast dev experience. Dev: Native ESM + esbuild, no bundling; Prod: Rollup esbuild Raw build speed (written in Go) 10–100× faster than JS tools; fewer advanced features Rollup Build a library Excellent tree-shaking, clean output (ESM/CJS/UMD). Why is Vite fast during development? Webpack bundles everything upfront, while Vite serves ESM on demand. The core idea of Vite Modern browsers support native ES modules. During development, Vite does not bundle but lets the browser import each module individually; Vite only transforms the modules that are requested (using esbuild for extremely fast processing). As a result, server startup and HMR are nearly instantaneous, regardless of project size. For production builds, Vite bundles using Rollup for optimization. How to choose a tool For building libraries → Rollup (clean output, good tree-shaking). For building new apps → Vite (excellent DX). For legacy/complex projects requiring specific plugins → Webpack. For raw speed in the pipeline → esbuild. Why does Vite start the dev server almost instantly even with large projects? Because it bundles 1000 times faster than Webpack. When the dev does NOT bundle — uses the browser's native ESM, only transforms the requested module. Because it does not require JavaScript. Because it runs on a dedicated server. Webpack bundles everything before running, so large projects start slowly. Vite leverages native ESM, only building modules requested by the browser (via esbuild) → instant startup & HMR.

handbookTitle: Designing a Frontend System from A to Z
text: Advanced Testing: Mock, Async & Contract After mastering the testing pyramid, here are the techniques that distinguish developers who write "runnable" tests from those who write "reliable" tests. Testing incorrectly is worse than not testing at all, as it creates a false sense of security. Mock vs Stub vs Spy — don't get confused. Concept What is it? Used when Stub Replace the function with a fixed return value. Need a dependency that returns predefined data (mock API returns an object). Spy Track how the ACTUAL function is called (number of times, parameters). To confirm whether the callback/analytics is called correctly. Mock A mock object has expectations about how it is called. Check interaction between modules, fail if called incorrectly. Fake Simple in-memory database implementation. Replace the heavy system with a lightweight version. Don't over-mock. Mocking everything makes tests only verify "the code calls the mocked function correctly" — it doesn't reflect real behavior. Prioritize mocking at system boundaries (network, time, storage), and keep the logic within the test running as real code. Testing asynchronous code & timers JS // Use fake timers to test debounce WITHOUT waiting in real time. vi.useFakeTimers(); const spy = vi.fn(); const debounced = debounce(spy, 300); debounced(); debounced(); // Call 2 times consecutively. vi.advanceTimersByTime(300); // "tua" 300ms expect(spy).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1); // runs only once Mock the network with MSW Mock Service Worker (MSW) intercepts requests at the network layer, so components use real fetch without needing code changes. The same mock works for both testing and development — preventing tests from "knowing too much" about how the API is called. Contract Testing — preventing "API changes without anyone knowing" When frontend and backend develop independently, contract tests ensure both sides still "understand each other": the frontend declares what response format it expects, and the backend confirms it provides that exact format. If the backend changes a field, the contract test fails immediately — catching the error before production. A high-scoring answer I test based on user behavior, mock at the network boundary using MSW, use fake timers for debounce/throttle, and apply contract tests for the FE-BE boundary. → This shows you understand testing at the correct layers. The main difference between "spy" and "stub" is that a spy records information about how a function is called (e.g., number of calls, arguments), while a stub replaces a function with a predefined behavior or return value, typically to isolate the code under test. There is no difference, just the name. Spy monitors how the real function is called; stub replaces the function with a predefined return value. Spy is only used for async, stub for sync. Stub is faster than spy. Spy observes the real function (how many times it is called, what parameters are passed) without altering its behavior; stub replaces the function entirely with a fixed value/implementation.

handbookTitle: Designing a Frontend System from A to Z
text: Storybook & Component Documentation Isolating components from the app enables efficient development, testing, and documentation. Storybook is the standard tool for building a living library for a design system. Why develop isolated components? Isolated development Build each component state (loading, error, empty, full) without running the entire app or creating complex data. Living document Each "story" is a live example. Designers and developers can view all variants, props, and usage patterns. Visual regression Take screenshots of each story, compare when changes occur → catch UI "breakage" that unit tests cannot detect. A11y audit Addon to check accessibility directly in the story: contrast, ARIA, focus order. Structure of a "story" JS // Button.stories.tsx — each export is one state export default { title: 'UI/Button', component: Button }; export const Primary = { args: { variant: 'primary', children: 'Save' } }; export const Loading = { args: { loading: true } }; export const Disabled = { args: { disabled: true } }; Story = test + docs + dev simultaneously A good story serves as documentation (for others to view), a playground (for developers to experiment), and input for visual regression tests. "Write once, use for three purposes" — this is why Storybook is worth investing in for teams with a design system. Systems thinking Mentioning Storybook when asked about design systems shows you're thinking about maintainability and collaboration, not just making code work. That's the mindset of someone building platform/infra for a team. What is the "3-in-1" benefit of a story in Storybook? Completely replace unit tests It serves as a living document, a development playground, and an input for visual regression. Make the bundle smaller. Automatically deploy the app A story is a live example → it serves as documentation, allows developers to test in isolation, and acts as a snapshot for visual regression testing.

handbookTitle: Designing a Frontend System from A to Z
text: Module Federation — executing micro-frontends This is the most common technical mechanism for implementing micro-frontends: allowing multiple apps to build and deploy independently while sharing code and rendering each other at runtime. Host & Remote The host loads the module from a remote source at runtime. Issues to address Challenge How to handle Duplicate dependency Declare shared resources (React, common libraries) to load once, avoiding multiple versions being downloaded. Version mismatch Set singleton: true for React → prevents two React instances from conflicting. Remote errors/slow performance Error boundary + fallback UI; don't let one remote crash the entire app. UI consistency Share the design system via a shared package. The cost to pay Module Federation adds significant complexity: managing shared dependencies, runtime versioning, difficulty debugging when remotes fail, and often worse performance than a monolith due to loading multiple runtimes. Only use it when the organizational benefits (independent teams) outweigh this cost. Alternative Not every micro-frontend requires Module Federation runtime. For lighter requirements: build-time integration (each team exports a package), iframe (strong isolation but limited UX), or web components. Choose based on the actual level of independence needed. Why is it necessary to declare React as a shared singleton in Module Federation? To make React run faster To avoid loading multiple React versions simultaneously — multiple React versions break hooks and context. Because Webpack requires To reduce the number of configuration lines If the host and remote each load a separate React instance, hooks and context will break (React requires a single instance). Setting `singleton: true` ensures only one React instance is shared.

handbookTitle: Designing a Frontend System from A to Z
text: Distributed Tracing & Alert Strategy When a request flows through FE → API gateway → multiple services, how do you identify which step is slow? Tracing connects the pieces into a single picture. And alert properly to avoid being "ignored" due to too many alerts. Trace, Span & Context Propagation A trace consists of multiple spans that are sequential/nested. The role of Frontend The frontend initializes a trace-id and sends it as a header (e.g., traceparent per W3C Trace Context standard) with every API call. This links user-facing errors/latency to backend logs — making it feasible to debug "why user X experienced slowness." Three Pillars of Observability Logs Discrete events have timestamps. Good for investigating a specific case in detail. Metrics Time-series aggregated metrics (p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate). Suitable for dashboards and alerts. Traces The journey of a request through services. Useful for identifying bottlenecks in a distributed system. Properly using alerts — combating "alert fatigue" The principle Meaning Alert on symptoms, not on root causes. Report "error rate > 2%" (affects users) instead of "high CPU" (may be harmless). Use percentile, not average. p95/p99 reflects the worst-case experience; averages hide the long tail. Actionable Each alert must have a clear action; if nothing can be done, do not alert. Reasonable threshold Too sensitive → false alarms (cry wolf); too loose → missed real incidents. Why p95 is more important than the average "Average 200ms" sounds fine, but if p99 is 5 seconds, then 1% of users are suffering — often the most important ones (heavy data users). Seniors always look at tail latency, not just the average. Why should alerts be based on p95/p99 latency instead of average latency? Because the average is more difficult to calculate. Averages hide the tail — a small group of users can have a very poor experience while the average still looks good. Since p99 is always smaller than the average Since the average does not measure latency A few extremely slow requests get "diluted" in the average, but p95/p99 exposes them. Tail latency often affects users with the most data.

handbookTitle: Designing a Frontend System from A to Z
text: Optimize Images & Resources Images often account for 50%+ of page weight. Proper optimization is the fastest way to improve LCP. This is a "low-hanging fruit" that many overlook. Image formats — choose the right one. Format Used when Notes AVIF Screenshots, background — top priority. Best compression, increasingly broad support. WebP Fallback for AVIF Smaller than JPEG/PNG by ~30% SVG Icon, logo, vector image Infinite resolution, small, can be styled with CSS. JPEG/PNG The final fallback PNG for images requiring transparency. Responsive images and lazy loading are techniques used to optimize web performance and improve user experience. Responsive images allow different image sizes to be served based on the user's device and screen resolution, ensuring that images are displayed at the appropriate size without unnecessary loading of large files on smaller screens. Lazy loading defers the loading of images until they are needed, typically when they come into the viewport. This reduces initial page load time and saves bandwidth, as images that are not immediately visible are not loaded until the user scrolls down to them. Implementing these techniques can significantly enhance the performance of a website, especially on mobile devices. HTML Always set width & height Declare width/height (or aspect-ratio) so the browser reserves space in advance — preventing layout shifts when images finish loading (improving CLS). Images without dimensions are the most common cause of CLS. LCP images should NOT be lazy-loaded. Images "above the fold" (typically LCP images) should use `loading="eager"` + `fetchpriority="high"`, and even preload. Lazy-loading them will worsen LCP. Only lazy-load images below the fold. Which images should have `loading="lazy"` applied? Large hero image at the top of the page (LCP image) The image is below the first screen; users have to scroll to see it. All images, without exception. The logo on the header Lazy-load defers image loading until near the viewport — good for off-screen images. Lazy-loading LCP/above-the-fold images will slow down LCP.

handbookTitle: Designing a Frontend System from A to Z
text: PWA, Service Worker & Offline-first A Service Worker is a background proxy between the app and the network, enabling the app to work offline, load instantly on subsequent visits, and receive push notifications. It is the foundation of an "app-like" experience. Where does the Service Worker stand? SW is a proxy between the app and the network. Cache strategy Strategy How it works "Matches" Cache First Fetch from cache first, only go to network if not available. Static resources (CSS, JS, fonts, logos) Network First Go to network first, use cache on error. Data needs to be fresh (feed, price) Stale-While-Revalidate Return cache immediately, while updating in the background. Avatar, content changes infrequently — fast + gradual updates. Trap: SW "stuck" on an old version Service Workers have their own lifecycle (install → waiting → activate). If updates are not handled properly, users may get stuck on an old version. A strategy of skip-waiting combined with a "New version available, reload?" notification is needed for smooth updates. Requirements of PWA To be installable as an app, you need HTTPS, a Web App Manifest (name, icon, theme), and a Service Worker. When these are in place, the browser shows an "Add to Home Screen" prompt. The most suitable caching strategy for feed data that must always be fresh but still needs a fallback when offline is **stale-while-revalidate**. This approach serves cached data immediately (stale) while fetching fresh data in the background, ensuring the user sees content even without a network connection. For critical freshness, combine it with a short max-age and a network-first strategy, falling back to cache only when the network fails. Cache First Network First Cache Only No caching at all. Network First prioritizes fetching fresh data from the network, only falling back to cache when offline or on error — suitable for feeds. Cache First returns stale content.

handbookTitle: Designing a Frontend System from A to Z
sectionTitle: Frontend in a large team scale.
text: Frontend in a large team scale. When a codebase has hundreds of developers, the issue is no longer individual technical skill but how to organize so that many people can work in parallel without conflicts or slowing each other down. Monorepo vs Polyrepo Criteria Monorepo Polyrepo Share the code. Easy — shared repo, simultaneous updates. Difficult — via npm package, versioning Synchronize changes A PR that fixes both the app and the library. Multiple PRs, multiple release steps Build/CI Need smart tools (Nx, Turborepo) to only build the changed parts. Simple, independent per repository. Team boundaries Need clear CODEOWNERS Naturally split by repo. Micro-frontends — when to use them. Don't use it just because it "sounds cool." Micro-frontends solve organizational problems (multiple teams deploying independently), not technical problems. The cost: complexity in shared dependencies, UI consistency, and performance (loading multiple runtimes). Only worthwhile when teams are large enough to block each other. Senior mindset "I'll start with a modular monolith with clear module boundaries. Only split into micro-frontends when there's evidence that teams are blocking each other during deployment." → shows you prioritize simpler solutions first. The most reasonable reason to adopt a micro-frontend architecture is to enable independent development, deployment, and scaling of frontend features by different teams, reducing coordination overhead and improving maintainability for large-scale applications. Make the app run faster. Reduce bundle size Allows multiple teams to develop and deploy independently without blocking each other. Because it is more modern. Micro-frontend is a solution for team organization/scaling issues, traded off by increased technical complexity and often worse performance. The main benefit is team independence.

handbookTitle: Designing a Frontend System from A to Z
text: Case Study: Chat Application (like Messenger) A classic interview question. A chat app combines nearly every topic: real-time, optimistic UI, virtualized list, offline, and state synchronization. We follow the RADIO framework. R — Requirements Functional Send/receive text messages in real-time, view conversation list, show delivery/read receipts (sent → delivered → read), typing indicators, media attachments (images/files), message history with infinite scroll upward. Non-Functional Message latency < 500ms (P99), 99.9% delivery guarantee, supports 10k concurrent users, smooth scroll through thousands of messages, works on 3G networks. Constraints Mobile-first (iOS/Android web), messages must queue offline and send on reconnect, support one-to-one and group chats up to 256 members. **Key clarification questions:** One-to-one only or group chat? Max group size? File/image attachments or text only? File size limit? Push notifications when app is backgrounded? End-to-end encryption required? A — Architecture Client architecture of chat Key design decision: WebSocket (not SSE) because chat is bidirectional — the user both sends and receives over the same persistent connection. The Local Queue stores outgoing messages while offline, draining them in order when the WebSocket reconnects. D — Data Model TypeScript — Normalized state interface Message { id: string; // server ID (replaces tempId after ack) tempId?: string; // client-generated, used for optimistic send conversationId: string; senderId: string; text: string; attachments: Attachment[]; status: 'sending' | 'sent' | 'delivered' | 'read' | 'failed'; sentAt: string; // ISO 8601 } // Normalized state: O(1) lookup, easy status updates interface ChatState { messages: { byId: Record<string, Message>; byConversation: Record<string, string[]>; // conversationId → messageIds }; conversations: { byId: Record<string, Conversation> }; ui: { typingUsers: Record<string, string[]>; // conversationId → userIds localQueue: Message[]; // pending offline messages }; } I — Interface (API & WebSocket Events) API contract // REST: initial data load GET /conversations → [{ id, participants, lastMessage, unreadCount }] GET /conversations/:id/messages?before=<cursor>&limit=30 → { messages: Message[], prevCursor: string | null } POST /media/upload-url → { uploadUrl: string; attachmentId: string } // WebSocket JSON frames // Client → Server { type: 'message', conversationId, tempId, text, attachmentIds } { type: 'read', conversationId, upToMessageId } { type: 'typing', conversationId, isTyping: true } // Server → Client { type: 'message', message: Message } // new incoming message { type: 'ack', tempId, serverId, status } // delivery confirmation { type: 'typing', conversationId, userId, isTyping } { type: 'read', conversationId, userId, upToMessageId } O — Optimizations Optimistic send Display message immediately with 'sending' status and tempId. On server ack, swap tempId → serverId. On error, mark 'failed' and show a retry button. Virtual list Only render messages within the viewport. Load more on reverse scroll (infinite scroll upward). Maintain scroll anchor when prepending history — CSS overflow-anchor or manual scrollTop adjustment. Reconnect & Sync WebSocket drops → exponential backoff (1s → 2s → 4s). On reconnection, fetch missed messages using the last known cursor, then drain the local queue in order. Typing & Presence Debounce typing events; emit at most once every 3s. Clear typing indicator after 5s of silence. Presence via heartbeat ping every 30s. **A11y**: `role="log"` + `aria-live="polite"` on message list — screen readers announce new messages without interrupting the user. **Security**: sanitize message content before rendering (prevent XSS via DOMPurify), validate file types server-side, use `Content-Security-Policy` headers. **Message ordering**: always sort by server timestamp on display — client clocks drift, so client timestamps are only for optimistic ordering. Ensure no data loss Each message has a client-generated idempotency key (tempId). When resending due to network loss, the same ID is used — the server deduplicates. Combine a local queue with IndexedDB so messages composed offline are sent when connectivity is restored. What the interviewer is listening for WebSocket vs SSE justification (chat needs two-way → WebSocket), how new messages are handled while the user is scrolled up through history (don't auto-scroll — show a 'scroll to bottom' badge), and how message order conflicts are resolved (always sort by server timestamp). Why should you use a client-generated id (idempotency key) for each message? To make the message shorter. So that when resending (due to network loss), the server can recognize it and avoid creating duplicate messages. To encode the message To avoid needing a database on the server. When the network is unstable, a client may resend a message that has already reached the server but has not yet received an acknowledgment. Using the same idempotency key helps the server deduplicate requests, ensuring exactly-once delivery.

handbookTitle: Designing a Frontend System from A to Z
text: Case Study: Autocomplete / Typeahead A small but extremely common problem because it tests: debounce, race condition, caching, and keyboard accessibility — all in one component. R — Requirements Functional Show dropdown suggestions as user types, navigate suggestions with keyboard (↑↓ Enter Esc), select suggestion to fill input, support async remote data source, show loading/empty states. Non-Functional Perceived response < 100ms for cached queries, < 300ms for fresh API requests. No stale/wrong results shown (race-condition-free). Accessible to keyboard and screen reader users. Constraints Works with mobile virtual keyboards, generic API (supports any data type via props), must be composable — caller provides data-fetching logic. **Key clarification questions:** Local static list or remote API? (changes architecture significantly) Maximum number of suggestions shown at once? (affects virtualization need) Should partial matches highlight the matching substring? Multi-select or single-select? A — Architecture & Data Flow Flow from key press to result D — Data Model TypeScript — state shape interface AutocompleteState { query: string; results: Suggestion[]; selectedIndex: number; // -1 = none, 0..n = highlighted item isOpen: boolean; isLoading: boolean; error: string | null; cache: Map<string, Suggestion[]>; // query → results, cleared on unmount } interface Suggestion { id: string; label: string; // displayed text metadata?: Record<string, unknown>; // caller-defined extra data } I — Interface (Props API) Props API + server contract interface AutocompleteProps<T extends Suggestion> { // Data source — caller owns the fetching logic fetchSuggestions: (query: string) => Promise<T[]>; // Display customization renderOption?: (item: T, isHighlighted: boolean) => ReactNode; getOptionLabel: (item: T) => string; // Behavior tuning debounceMs?: number; // default 300 minChars?: number; // default 1 — no fetch until N chars typed maxResults?: number; // default 10 // Controlled mode value?: T | null; onChange?: (item: T | null) => void; // Slots placeholder?: string; emptyMessage?: string; loadingMessage?: string; } // Server endpoint GET /search?q={query}&limit=10 → { suggestions: [{ id, label, ...metadata }] } O — Key Optimizations Handling Race Conditions Race condition + cache useEffect(() => { if (query.length < minChars) return; // Check cache first if (cache.has(query)) { setResults(cache.get(query)!); return; } const controller = new AbortController(); setIsLoading(true); fetchSuggestions(query, { signal: controller.signal }) .then(results => { cache.set(query, results); // store in session cache setResults(results); }) .catch(e => { if (e.name !== 'AbortError') setError(e.message); }) .finally(() => setIsLoading(false)); // Cancel the in-flight request when query changes or unmount return () => controller.abort(); }, [query]); Accessibility — the point many candidates miss Use the ARIA combobox pattern: `role="combobox"` on the input with `aria-expanded`, `aria-autocomplete="list"`, `aria-controls` pointing to the listbox. Set `aria-activedescendant` to the ID of the highlighted option. Keyboard: ↑↓ to navigate, Enter to select, Esc to close and restore original value, Tab to close. Query caching Cache results by query in a Map. When the user deletes and retypes the same word, return immediately from cache — no API call. Combine with 300ms debounce to reduce requests by ~80%. For very long lists (100+ suggestions), add virtualization to the dropdown. In autocomplete, a race condition occurs when the response from an earlier request arrives after the response from a later request, causing the UI to display outdated results. The correct way to handle this is to use a cancellation mechanism, such as an AbortController in fetch, or by tracking the latest request with a counter or timestamp to ignore stale responses. When typing too slowly; handle by increasing debounce. When the response of an old query arrives after a new query and overwrites it; handle by using AbortController to cancel the old request. When the cache is too large; clear the cache. When the dropdown is too long; virtualize the list. A request sent earlier may return later than a later request, causing old results to overwrite new ones. Canceling the old request with AbortController (or ignoring responses that don't match the current query) is the standard approach.

handbookTitle: Designing a Frontend System from A to Z
sectionTitle: Case Study: Photo Gallery (like Google Photos)
text: Case Study: Photo Gallery (like Google Photos) The problem of smoothly displaying thousands of images. Check: virtualization for the grid, lazy loading, responsive images, and lightbox. The core principle is "only work with what the user sees." R — Requirements Functional Browse photos in a responsive masonry/justified grid, infinite scroll to load more, click photo to open fullscreen lightbox with prev/next navigation, search/filter by date or album. Non-Functional Above-the-fold images visible in < 1s, smooth 60fps scroll with 10,000+ photos, no CLS when images load, lightbox opens in < 200ms. Constraints Various image aspect ratios (portrait, landscape, square), mobile-first with pinch-to-zoom in lightbox, bandwidth-conscious (serve thumbnails; full res only on demand). **Key clarification questions:** Fixed grid (equal tiles) or justified layout (variable width, consistent row height)? User's own photos only or shared albums? Upload feature required or read-only gallery? Max photos per gallery? (affects pagination strategy) A — Architecture & Key Techniques Virtualized grid: only render images within the viewport. Key design decisions: Server must return width and height for each photo so the browser can reserve the correct space before the image loads — essential for a CLS-free justified layout. Virtual DOM recycling keeps memory flat regardless of gallery size. Responsive thumbnails Server generates multiple sizes (200px, 400px, 800px). srcset + sizes attributes ensure each device loads the correct resolution. Full-res loaded only on lightbox open. LQIP blur-up Display average color or blur-up placeholder while loading → creates a fast feel and prevents layout shifts. Server returns blurDataUrl alongside each photo. DOM node recycling When scrolling, reuse virtual nodes that have left the screen instead of creating new ones → reduces GC pressure and keeps memory stable. Lightbox preload When opening an image, preload the adjacent prev/next images to enable smooth navigation without latency. D — Data Model TypeScript — state shape interface Photo { id: string; url: string; // full-resolution URL (lazy-loaded in lightbox) thumbnailUrl: string; // 400px thumbnail URL blurDataUrl: string; // tiny base64 LQIP placeholder width: number; // original pixel width — required for layout calc height: number; // original pixel height takenAt: string; // ISO 8601 alt: string; } interface GalleryState { photos: { byId: Record<string, Photo>; displayOrder: string[]; // ordered photo IDs nextCursor: string | null; }; layout: PhotoLayout[]; // pre-calculated positions (top, left, w, h) lightbox: { isOpen: boolean; currentId: string | null; isTransitioning: boolean; }; } I — Interface (API) API contract // Paginated photo list GET /photos?cursor=<c>&limit=30&albumId=<id> → { photos: [{ id, thumbnailUrl, blurDataUrl, width, height, takenAt, alt }], nextCursor: string | null } // Full-res on demand (only fetched when lightbox opens) GET /photos/:id → { ...Photo, url: string } // includes full-resolution URL // Upload (if required) POST /photos/upload-url → { uploadUrl: string; photoId: string } // Client PUTs binary directly to CDN via uploadUrl O — Optimizations **Justified layout math**: server returns width/height per photo. Client runs a layout algorithm (e.g., Google's bin-packing) to compute row heights and positions. Cache layout to avoid recalculation on every scroll. **Scroll anchor on load more**: when fetching older photos above, record `scrollTop` before appending and restore it after to prevent the viewport jumping. **IntersectionObserver** on bottom sentinel → fetch next batch when within 300px of fold. **Lightbox keyboard a11y**: trap focus inside lightbox (`Tab`/`Shift+Tab`), `ArrowLeft`/`ArrowRight` navigate, `Escape` closes, `role="dialog"` + `aria-label`. **Pinch-to-zoom**: use native CSS `touch-action: manipulation` + a library like `react-zoom-pan-pinch` for mobile lightbox. What the interviewer pays attention to How to calculate justified grid layout when images have different aspect ratios (server must return dimensions), how to maintain scroll position when loading more images, and what happens when a user opens a lightbox for a photo not yet loaded at full-res (show blur-up, load in background, fade in). Why is virtualization important for a gallery of 10,000 images? To make the image sharper. Only render images within the viewport → lightweight DOM, smooth scrolling, memory does not bloat with the number of images. To load all images faster To use less CSS Rendering all 10,000 image nodes makes the DOM heavy, consumes memory, and causes lag when scrolling. Virtualization renders only the visible portion, keeping the DOM lightweight regardless of the total number of images.

handbookTitle: Designing a Frontend System from A to Z
text: Case Study: Infinite Data Table A massive data table (like Airtable, financial spreadsheets) with millions of rows and many columns. Check: bidirectional virtualization, server-side sort/filter, sticky header/column, and inline editing. R — Requirements Functional Display millions of rows with 50+ columns, sort by any column, multi-column filter, inline cell editing, sticky first column + header row, column resize/reorder, row selection, CSV export. Non-Functional < 16ms frame budget during scroll (60fps), < 500ms for sort/filter operations, support 1M rows × 50 columns without browser freeze, optimistic inline edits. Constraints Desktop-first (financial users), rows may have variable height (text wrap), must not load all data into memory, real-time updates from other users editing. **Key clarification questions:** Fixed or variable row height? (variable height dramatically increases virtualization complexity) Real-time collaborative editing or single-user? How many columns max? Are columns user-configurable? Export format requirements? (CSV, Excel, PDF) A — Architecture Only render cells within the visible area (both rows & columns). Key design decision: virtualize both rows and columns — a table with 50 columns and 1M rows could generate 50M DOM nodes without virtualization. The render window is typically ~20 rows × visible columns, with a small buffer. Libraries like @tanstack/virtual or ag-grid handle this well. D — Data Model TypeScript — state shape interface Column { id: string; label: string; type: 'text' | 'number' | 'date' | 'select'; width: number; // pixel width — resizable pinned?: 'left'; // sticky column } interface Row { id: string; cells: Record<string, CellValue>; // columnId → value _version: number; // optimistic concurrency } interface TableState { columns: Column[]; rows: { byId: Record<string, Row>; order: string[] }; sort: { columnId: string; direction: 'asc' | 'desc' } | null; filters: Record<string, FilterValue>; cursor: string | null; // for server-side pagination editingCell: { rowId: string; columnId: string } | null; } I — Interface (API) API contract // Never load all rows — server handles sort/filter/paginate GET /rows ?sort=price:desc &filter={"status":"active","price":{"gte":100}} &cursor=<c> &limit=100 → { rows: Row[], totalCount: number, nextCursor: string | null } // Inline cell edit — optimistic with version check PATCH /rows/:id body: { cells: { [columnId]: newValue }, _version: number } → { row: Row } // 409 Conflict if version mismatch // Real-time updates (SSE or WebSocket) GET /rows/changes (EventSource) ← data: { type: 'update', rowId, cells, _version } O — Optimizations Why use sort/filter on the server side? Sorting 1 million rows on the client will block the main thread. The server (with indexed database queries) handles this in milliseconds and only returns the page of data the client needs. Client-side sort/filter is only appropriate when the entire dataset is already loaded (< ~5,000 rows). **Optimistic cell edit**: update cell in local state immediately, send PATCH in background, rollback on 409 conflict (another user edited same row). **Debounce column resize**: update column width in local state on every mouse move, but only persist to server on `mouseup`. **Web Worker for large exports**: CSV generation for 100k rows blocks the main thread. Offload to a Web Worker or stream the download from the server. **Row selection**: track selected row IDs in a Set, not booleans on each row — avoids re-rendering unselected rows on selection change. **A11y**: use `role="grid"`, `role="row"`, `role="gridcell"`, arrow key navigation between cells, announce sort direction changes with `aria-sort`. Trap: dynamic row height If each row has different height (text wrap), virtualization becomes much harder — you need to measure and cache actual heights after render, or use estimation with adjustment. Fixed row height is dramatically simpler. Confirm with requirements. With a table of 1 million rows, where should sorting/filtering be done? Load everything to the client and sort using JavaScript. On the server (with an indexed database), the client only requests a page of sorted/filtered data. In localStorage No need to sort. Loading and sorting 1 million rows on the client freezes the UI. A server with an index processes quickly and only returns the "window" of data the client is viewing. Client-side sorting is only suitable for small datasets.

handbookTitle: Designing a Frontend System from A to Z
text: Case Study: Video Player (like YouTube) Smooth video playback at all network speeds. Tests understanding of adaptive bitrate streaming (HLS/DASH), buffering, and building custom controls with accessibility. R — Requirements Functional Play/pause/seek, volume + mute, playback speed (0.5×–2×), quality selection (auto + manual), fullscreen, captions/subtitles, chapter markers, watch progress saved server-side. Non-Functional Playback starts within 2s, no rebuffering on stable 4G+, quality auto-adapts to bandwidth, supports 4K/1080p/720p/480p, works on iOS Safari (HLS native) and desktop (DASH via MSE). Constraints Must work on iOS Safari (which requires HLS, not DASH), custom player UI (native controls are not brandable), no autoplay with audio (browser policy + a11y). **Key clarification questions:** Live stream or VOD (Video on Demand)? DRM (Digital Rights Management) required? Captions mandatory (legal requirement in some regions)? Picture-in-picture support required? A — Architecture The video is divided into chunks of multiple qualities, and the player selects based on network conditions. Key design decision: use an established ABR library ( hls.js for HLS, dash.js for DASH) rather than implementing ABR from scratch. The player UI is a custom React layer on top of a native <video> element — native controls are hidden, custom ones overlay it. D — Data Model TypeScript — player state interface PlayerState { // Playback isPlaying: boolean; currentTime: number; // seconds duration: number; buffered: [number, number][]; // array of [start, end] buffered ranges // Quality quality: 'auto' | '1080p' | '720p' | '480p' | '360p'; currentBandwidth: number; // estimated kbps // Controls volume: number; // 0..1 isMuted: boolean; playbackRate: number; // 0.5 | 1 | 1.25 | 1.5 | 2 isFullscreen: boolean; // Captions captionsEnabled: boolean; activeCaptionTrack: string | null; // e.g. 'en', 'fr' // Persistence savedPosition: number; // loaded from server on init } I — Interface (API) API contract // Video metadata + stream manifest GET /videos/:id → { id, title, duration, thumbnailUrl, manifestUrl: string, // .m3u8 (HLS) or .mpd (DASH) captions: [{ lang, label, url }], chapters: [{ startTime, title }] } // Player saves progress every 15s (or on pause/unload) POST /videos/:id/progress body: { position: number } // seconds → 204 No Content // Captions fetched on demand GET <captionUrl> → WebVTT file // HLS manifest from CDN GET <manifestUrl> → m3u8 playlist GET <chunkUrl> → .ts segment (fetched by hls.js internally) O — Optimizations Buffer & States Concept Meaning HLS / DASH Two streaming standards divide video into chunks + manifest. HLS is popular on Apple, DASH is an open standard. Buffer ahead Preload several chunks to prevent lag when the network fluctuates. Startup time Start at a low level to play fast, then gradually increase as the network is measured. MSE (Media Source Extensions) The browser API that allows JavaScript to "load" chunks into a video element — the foundation of an ABR player. The core trade-off of ABR High quality vs. rebuffering risk. ABR always prioritizes uninterrupted playback over maximum quality — a single rebuffer stall kills user experience more than watching at 480p. Starting at low quality and ramping up is the standard strategy. **Preload next segment**: buffer several chunks ahead of playhead to absorb bandwidth spikes. Tune buffer goal (e.g., 15s) for VOD; use smaller buffer for live streams to reduce latency. **Thumbnail scrubbing**: pre-generate a sprite sheet of thumbnails at 1-per-second intervals. When user hovers the scrubber, show the sprite at that timestamp without seeking. **Save position on unload**: use `visibilitychange` + `pagehide` events (not `beforeunload` — unreliable on mobile) to POST progress to server. **Reduced motion**: respect `prefers-reduced-motion` — disable animated transitions in controls. **Performance**: hide custom controls overlay during playback (opacity:0, pointer-events:none) — a transparent overlay intercepts events but adds no paint cost. A11y for player — the full checklist Space = play/pause, ←/→ = seek ±5s, ↑/↓ = volume, F = fullscreen, C = toggle captions. All controls need `aria-label` (e.g., aria-label="Play"). Progress bar = `role="slider"` with `aria-valuenow`, `aria-valuemin`, `aria-valuemax`. Never autoplay with audio — browser policy blocks it and it violates WCAG 1.4.2. When the user's network drops mid-stream, Adaptive Bitrate Streaming (ABR) works by detecting the decrease in available bandwidth through client-side monitoring. The player then automatically switches to a lower-bitrate video segment, reducing quality to prevent buffering. This process is seamless, as the video is divided into small chunks encoded at multiple bitrates, and the player requests the next chunk at the appropriate level based on real-time network conditions. Stop the video and report the error. The next chunk is loaded at a lower quality level, and the video continues without interruption. Reload the entire video from the beginning. Switch to static image The video is divided into chunks at multiple quality levels. When the network drops, the player selects the next chunk at a lower quality to maintain continuous playback — prioritizing no buffering over maximum quality.

handbookTitle: Designing a Frontend System from A to Z
sectionTitle: Case Study: Collaborative Editing (like Google Docs)
text: Case Study: Collaborative Editing (like Google Docs) The hardest and most "valuable" problem: multiple users editing the same document in real-time without overwriting each other. Tests understanding of OT vs CRDT, presence, and conflict resolution. R — Requirements Functional Real-time collaborative text editing, see other users' cursors and selections, rich text formatting (bold, italic, headings, lists), comments/suggestions, version history with restore, offline editing (changes sync on reconnect). Non-Functional Local keystrokes feel instantaneous (< 50ms), changes from other users appear within 500ms, convergence guaranteed — all users see the same document after edits settle, no data loss on network drop. Constraints Support 50+ concurrent editors on the same document, works offline and syncs on reconnect, document must be stored persistently (not just in memory), must handle browser crashes gracefully. **Key clarification questions:** Rich text (Google Docs) or plain text/code (like Replit)? Max concurrent editors per document? Is offline editing required? (fundamentally changes the architecture) Comment threads and suggestions, or just live editing? A — Architecture & Core Challenge Core issue: concurrent editing Two people editing simultaneously — how to avoid overwriting? Key design decision: use an established CRDT library ( Yjs with y-websocket provider) rather than implementing OT/CRDT from scratch. Yjs handles conflict resolution, offline sync, and presence out of the box. Custom OT implementations are notoriously difficult to get correct. D — Data Model TypeScript — Yjs-based state // Using Yjs CRDT import * as Y from 'yjs'; const ydoc = new Y.Doc(); const ytext = ydoc.getText('content'); // shared text with CRDT semantics // Client state interface CollabState { syncStatus: 'synced' | 'pending' | 'offline'; localVersion: number; collaborators: { [userId: string]: { name: string; color: string; // unique color per user cursor: number | null; // character offset in document selection: { from: number; to: number } | null; }; }; comments: Comment[]; pendingOps: Y.UpdateType[]; // buffered while offline } // Version history snapshot interface Snapshot { id: string; createdAt: string; createdBy: string; description: string; stateVector: Uint8Array; // Yjs state vector for this point in time } I — Interface (WebSocket Protocol) WebSocket + REST API // WebSocket (y-websocket protocol) // Initial sync Client → Server: { type: 'sync-step-1', stateVector: Uint8Array } Server → Client: { type: 'sync-step-2', update: Uint8Array } // missing ops // Incremental updates Client → Server: { type: 'update', update: Uint8Array } // local edit Server → Client: { type: 'update', update: Uint8Array } // remote edit // Presence (cursor/selection — ephemeral, not persisted) Client → Server: { type: 'awareness', state: { cursor, selection, user } } Server → Client: { type: 'awareness', changes: { [clientId]: state } } // REST: document management GET /docs/:id → { id, title, createdAt, collaborators } GET /docs/:id/history → { snapshots: Snapshot[] } POST /docs/:id/snapshot → create a named checkpoint GET /docs/:id/snapshot/:snapshotId → { content: Uint8Array } OT vs CRDT — two approaches. Criteria OT (Operational Transformation) CRDT The idea Transform operations concurrently to maintain consistency. Self-merging data structure, no transformation needed. Do we need a central server? Often requires (coordinating the order) Optional — suitable for P2P/offline Complexity Complex logic transformations are difficult to get right. Simpler in theory, but requires more metadata. Used by Google Docs (traditional) Figma, many new apps, Yjs/Automerge Presence Other users' cursor & selection sent via private channel (no persistence needed), throttle to reduce traffic. Offline editing Save local operations when offline; when back online, merge using CRDT/OT — no data loss. Version history Save snapshot + operation sequence to rewind history and restore. Local-first Apply changes locally immediately (optimistic), sync in the background → no typing lag. Why not use "last write wins"? The simplest approach — last writer wins — overwrites the other person's text. OT/CRDT ensures both concurrent operations are preserved and all clients converge to the same state. This is the difference between a "toy" and a real product. O — Optimizations **Local-first rendering**: apply keystrokes to local Yjs document immediately (no round-trip) → zero typing lag. Sync to server in background. **Presence throttling**: send cursor position updates at most 50ms intervals (throttle) — presence is ephemeral and lossy delivery is acceptable. **Offline buffer**: store pending Yjs updates in IndexedDB. On reconnect, replay in order — Yjs merges them correctly with server state. **Large document performance**: use a ProseMirror or CodeMirror editor that supports incremental rendering — never re-render the entire document on each change. **A11y**: announce collaborator joins/leaves via `aria-live="polite"`, expose cursor positions in a non-obtrusive way, ensure the editor remains keyboard-navigable. **Security**: validate all operations server-side (reject ops from users without write permission), use CRDT for conflict resolution but authorize each op independently. How to make an impression in the O part State that this is a 'convergence in distributed systems' problem. Compare OT vs CRDT with clear trade-offs. Mention local-first + offline editing. Bring up presence throttling and the ephemeral vs. persistent data split. No need to code transform algorithms — understanding the principles and trade-offs is sufficient for the FE round. Why does collaborative editing NOT use the "last write wins" strategy? Because it is too slow. Because it overwrites other people's changes; OT/CRDT preserves all concurrent operations and ensures convergence. Because the browser does not support it. Because it consumes a lot of memory. "Last write wins" causes one person's operation to overwrite another's → data loss. OT and CRDT merge concurrent operations so that no data is lost and all clients converge to the same result.

sectionTitle: Case Study: Designing a News Feed
text: Case Study: Designing a News Feed Applying RADIO to a classic problem: designing a Facebook/Twitter-style feed. This is a template you can reuse for most feed-based questions. R — Requirements Functional View personalized feed (infinite scroll), create posts (text + images/video), like/comment/share, see new-posts notification pill, real-time update when new content arrives. Non-Functional LCP < 2.5s on mobile 3G, 60fps smooth scroll, WCAG AA accessibility, works on intermittent connectivity, supports 1M+ posts in history. Constraints 60%+ mobile users (Android Chrome 90+, Safari 14+), post-login only so SEO is not a concern, internationalized UI (LTR + RTL languages). **Key clarification questions:** Personalized algorithmic feed or strictly chronological? Who can post — all users or verified accounts only? Video support? (affects CDN strategy and player complexity) Real-time updates required, or eventual consistency (5s poll) acceptable? Offline read access required? A — Architecture News Feed Architecture Key design decisions: FeedContainer is ‘smart’ (owns all data fetching + pagination state); PostCard is ‘dumb’ (pure rendering from props) — trivially testable and reusable. VirtualizedList is critical: without it, 1,000+ posts render all DOM nodes at once and lag on mobile. Rendering pattern: CSR + React Query — feed is post-login and personalized, so SSR adds server cost with no SEO benefit. D — Data Model TypeScript — Normalized state interface Post { id: string; authorId: string; text: string; mediaUrls: string[]; // CDN URLs for images/video thumbnails likeCount: number; commentCount: number; likedByMe: boolean; createdAt: string; // ISO 8601 } // Normalized client state — avoids duplication across feed + profile views interface FeedState { posts: { byId: Record; feedOrder: string[]; // ordered post IDs nextCursor: string | null; }; users: { byId: Record }; ui: { composerDraft: string; newPostCount: number; // from SSE — drives the "N new posts" pill }; } Why normalize? Without normalization, updating a user’s name requires patching every post that references them. With normalization, a single users.byId[userId].name update propagates everywhere automatically — critical for large feeds where the same user may appear in hundreds of posts. I — Interface (API) API contract // REST endpoints GET /feed?cursor=&limit=10 → { posts: Post[], users: User[], nextCursor: string | null } POST /posts body: { text: string; mediaIds?: string[] } → { post: Post } POST /posts/:id/like → { likeCount: number; likedByMe: true } DELETE /posts/:id/like → { likeCount: number; likedByMe: false } // Two-step media upload — keeps API server lean POST /media/upload-url → { uploadUrl: string; mediaId: string } // pre-signed S3 URL // Client PUTs binary directly to CDN via uploadUrl // Server-Sent Events for real-time new post count GET /feed/updates (EventSource) ← data: { type: ‘new_posts’, count: 3 } // drives the "3 new posts" pill Component API // PostCard — dumb component, no internal async state interface PostCardProps { post: Post; author: User; onLike: (postId: string) => void; onComment: (postId: string) => void; onShare: (postId: string) => void; } // FeedContainer — smart component, owns data fetching const { data, fetchNextPage } = useInfiniteQuery({ queryKey: [‘feed’], queryFn: ({ pageParam }) => fetchFeed({ cursor: pageParam }), staleTime: 30_000, // 30s before background refetch }); O — Optimizations **Virtualization**: windowing with `react-virtuoso` — DOM stays at ~10–15 nodes regardless of feed length. **IntersectionObserver** on sentinel element → auto-triggers next page fetch. **Images**: LQIP blur-up placeholder + `srcset` for responsive sizes + explicit `width`/`height` → zero CLS. **Optimistic UI**: like/comment update immediately, rollback on API error. **New posts pill**: SSE pushes count → show pill, never auto-insert (would shift user’s reading position). **Resilience**: stale cache shown offline, exponential backoff retry on reconnect. **Code splitting**: PostComposer and media viewer lazily loaded — excluded from critical path bundle. **A11y**: `aria-live="polite"` region for new-post count, `role="article"` on PostCard, keyboard-focusable like/comment buttons. Optimistic UI — React Query // Optimistic like — instant feedback, rollback on error function handleLike(postId: string) { const prevData = queryClient.getQueryData([‘post’, postId]); queryClient.setQueryData([‘post’, postId], (old: Post) => ({ ...old, likedByMe: !old.likedByMe, likeCount: old.likedByMe ? old.likeCount - 1 : old.likeCount + 1, })); likeMutation.mutate(postId, { onError: () => queryClient.setQueryData([‘post’, postId], prevData), // rollback }); } CLS-free images // CLS-free image with LQIP blur-up placeholder // Server returns blurDataUrl: a tiny ~20×20 base64-encoded image How to "score points" in the O part Don’t list everything. Pick 2–3 optimizations most relevant to the finalized requirements (e.g., because smoothness on mobile is needed → virtualization + responsive images) and dive deep into them. Depth over breadth. In the News Feed, why should we show a "X new posts" pill instead of automatically inserting new posts at the top of the list? To use less bandwidth. Avoid layout shift (CLS) to prevent users from losing their reading position; give them control. Since SSE does not allow automatic insertion To make coding easier Auto-inserting content at the top pushes the user's current reading position down (bad CLS, causes annoyance). Use a pill so they can actively tap when ready — much better UX.

sectionTitle: Interview Checklist — Print and Review Quickly
text: Interview Checklist — Print and Review Quickly A set of "reflexes" to ensure you don't miss anything in the interview. Practice until it becomes second nature. 60-Minute Agenda Suggested time allocation Always mention "trade-off" questions. Performance vs Complexity Which optimizations are worth the effort? Measure before optimizing. CSR vs SSR Balance between SEO/front-end performance and server cost/complexity. Real-time vs Simple WebSocket is powerful but complex; polling is sufficient for many cases. Cache vs Freshness Stale-while-revalidate balances both. Signs of a strong candidate (1) Ask clarifying questions before solving. (2) Draw clear diagrams. (3) Always mention trade-offs, never say "always use X". (4) Proactively address a11y, error handling, and performance. (5) Manage time wisely, know when to dive deep. Comprehensive flashcard set RADIO stands for "Radio Detection and Ranging". Requirements · Architecture · Data model · Interface (API) · Optimizations. 4 types of state? Server state · Local state · Global UI state · URL state. Each type has its own tools. What are the 3 Core Web Vitals? LCP (<2.5s) · INP (<200ms) · CLS (<0.1) Optimistic UI is a design pattern where the user interface immediately reflects the expected outcome of an action, without waiting for confirmation from the server. This creates a faster, more responsive user experience. If the server later rejects the action, the UI rolls back to the previous state and displays an error. Update the UI immediately before the server responds, rollback on error → instant feel. When to use WebSocket? For two-way, low-latency communication: chat, collaboration, gaming, trading. How do you prevent XSS? Escape output, avoid dangerouslySetInnerHTML, sanitize (DOMPurify), CSP, HttpOnly cookies.

handbookTitle: Designing a Frontend System from A to Z
text: Question bank summary Mix multiple topics to test overall knowledge. Answer first, then view the explanation. Try to explain "why" yourself before clicking. The biggest issue with pure CSR for a marketing website is what? Poor SEO and slow initial content display (white screen while loading JS). Cannot use CSS Does not run on mobile. Does not support JavaScript CSR returns an empty HTML shell, then loads JS and fetches data, causing an initial white screen and difficulty for crawlers → bad for the SEO of marketing pages. Which technique is most effective at reducing initial JS load time for large apps? Write shorter code. Code splitting + lazy loading by route/component Using many global variables. Inline all CSS Code splitting only loads the JavaScript needed for the current screen, significantly reducing the initial bundle size → faster FCP/LCP. GraphQL best solves the problem of over-fetching and under-fetching data in REST APIs. Over-fetching / under-fetching — the client declares exactly the fields it needs. Make the server run faster Absolute security Eliminate the need for caching. GraphQL allows clients to fetch exactly the data they need with a single query, reducing over/under-fetching. However, caching is more complex compared to REST. Where should the selected filter and tab be stored so that sharing the link and the back/forward buttons work correctly? useState in the component Redux global store URL state (query parameters) localStorage State that needs to be "shareable" and synchronized with browser history should be placed in the URL. When users copy the link, they get the exact state. The lightest and most suitable mechanism for displaying push notifications from the server is? WebSocket (always) SSE — server pushes one-way, auto-reconnect, runs over HTTP. Reload the page every second. Cannot be done on the web. Notification only requires server-to-client (one-way). SSE is lighter than WebSocket, has auto-reconnect, and runs over standard HTTP. Which attribute is used to announce dynamic content (e.g., "added to cart") to screen readers? aria-hidden aria-live (polite/assertive) **tabindex** role="alert" aria-live tells the screen reader to read content when that region changes without requiring focus. Polite waits until the current reading finishes, while assertive interrupts immediately. The most secure way to store session tokens against XSS is? localStorage JavaScript global variable Cookies with HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite In the URL localStorage/JS variables can both be read by scripts → dangerous if XSS occurs. HttpOnly cookies prevent JS from reading them, and combining Secure + SameSite mitigates both XSS and CSRF. Reading `element.offsetHeight` immediately after changing the styles of multiple elements will cause what? No effect. Forced synchronous layout — layout thrashing if repeated. Delete all CSS Automatically optimize paint Reading layout properties forces the browser to recalculate layout immediately to return accurate values. Interleaving reads and writes in a loop causes thrashing. Batch reads first, then writes. Between Promise.then and setTimeout(fn, 0), which runs first? Promise.then — because microtasks are cleared before macrotasks. setTimeout — because it's set to 0ms Random At the same time After each macrotask, the event loop clears the entire microtask queue before fetching the next macrotask. Promises (microtasks) always run before setTimeout (macrotasks). According to the testing pyramid, unit tests should make up the largest number of tests. E2E Unit (and integration) — fast, cheap, stable. Visual regression Manual testing The testing pyramid recommends many unit/integration tests (fast, cheap) at the bottom, and few E2E tests (slow, expensive, prone to flakiness) at the top. The core difference between "lab data" and "field data" is what? There is no difference. Lab = stable simulated environment (Lighthouse); Field = measured from real users (RUM/CrUX) Lab is always more precise than field. The field only runs on localhost. Lab data is good for debugging under controlled conditions; field data reflects real user experiences across diverse devices/networks and is what Google uses for ranking. Tree-shaking requires ES module syntax (import/export) to work effectively, as it relies on static analysis to determine which exports are used and which can be removed. Code must be written in TypeScript. Use ES modules (static import/export) so the bundler can analyze unused code. Must use CommonJS `require`. Disable minification Tree-shaking relies on static analysis of ES module import/export to eliminate dead code. Dynamic CommonJS is difficult to analyze, resulting in poor tree-shaking. The most common cause of CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) related to images is missing explicit width and height attributes on image elements. The image is too sharp. Images without declared width/height cause content to jump when the image finishes loading. Use the WebP format. The image has alt text. Without dimensions, the browser does not reserve space, and content below gets pushed down when the image loads → CLS. Declare width/height or aspect-ratio. What is the role of a Service Worker? Increase the device's CPU speed A background proxy intercepts requests, manages cache, and enables offline support and push notifications. Replace the backend server Server-side rendering of HTML A Service Worker is a background script that sits between the app and the network, controlling cache and requests — forming the foundation for offline-first functionality and push notifications. Why should chat use WebSocket instead of SSE? WebSocket is more secure. Chat requires real-time two-way communication; WebSocket supports both sending and receiving, while SSE is only one-way server-to-client. SSE does not run on the browser. WebSocket does not require a connection. Continuous chat sends and receives from both sides. WebSocket is a full-duplex channel that fits this use case; SSE only pushes one-way, so it's more suitable for notifications/feeds. In conclusion FE System Design has no single correct answer. Practice the mindset of: clarify → structure → trade-offs → deep dive. Revisit the diagrams and flashcards here regularly; spaced repetition is the best way to retain knowledge. Wishing you a successful interview! 🚀

handbookTitle: Optimization Deep Dive — Staff-Level Performance Handbook
text: Measurement & Profiling Before you touch a single line of code, you must identify the real bottleneck — not the one you think exists. At scale, optimizing the wrong thing wastes engineering time and can degrade user experience. This section teaches you to measure precisely, distinguish lab from field data, and apply a disciplined measure → optimize → verify loop. Core Web Vitals: The North Star Metrics Google's Core Web Vitals define user-centric thresholds: LCP ( INP ( CLS ( TTFB ( FCP ( meeting thresholds in the lab does not guarantee field performance . LCP: Largest Contentful Paint — measures perceived load speed. Optimize by preloading critical resources, reducing render-blocking CSS/JS, and using a CDN. INP: Interaction to Next Paint — measures responsiveness. Optimize by breaking long tasks (<50ms), using web workers, and debouncing input handlers. CLS: Cumulative Layout Shift — measures visual stability. Optimize by setting explicit dimensions on images/ads, using font-display: swap, and avoiding dynamic content injection above the fold. TTFB: Time to First Byte — measures server response. Optimize with edge caching, server-side rendering, and reducing backend latency. FCP: First Contentful Paint — measures first visual. Optimize by inlining critical CSS and deferring non-critical scripts. Lab Data vs Field Data: Why They Disagree Lab data (Lighthouse, WebPageTest) runs in a controlled environment with a consistent device and network. Field data (RUM, Chrome UX Report) captures real user conditions — slow networks, low-end devices, ad blockers. They disagree because lab data measures potential; field data measures reality . A staff engineer uses both: lab for debugging and regression detection, field for prioritization and impact assessment. Aspect Lab Data Field Data Environment Controlled (e.g., Moto G4, Slow 3G) Real user devices, networks, locations Metrics Synthetic scores (Lighthouse performance) Real user percentiles (p75, p95) Use Case Debugging, CI gates, regression detection Prioritization, user impact, long-term trends Limitation May not reflect real-world variability Noisy, requires sufficient sample size Senior Signal: Always Measure First A junior engineer says 'I think the bottleneck is the hero image.' A staff engineer says 'Let me check the field data — if LCP is above 2.5s for 75% of users, then we profile the main thread to see if it's network or rendering.' Never guess; always measure with real data. Chrome DevTools Performance Panel: Flame Charts & Long Tasks The Performance panel records a timeline of main thread activity. Look for long tasks (>50ms) that block the main thread — these cause INP issues. Flame charts show function call stacks; identify expensive scripts, layout thrashing, or excessive garbage collection. Use the Bottom-Up tab to sort by total time and find the heaviest functions. JavaScript // Simulate a long task that blocks the main thread function blockMainThread(ms) { const start = performance.now(); while (performance.now() - start < ms) { // Busy wait — never do this in production } } // Use requestIdleCallback to defer non-critical work requestIdleCallback(() => { // Process analytics or logging here }, { timeout: 2000 }); JavaScript // Measure long tasks programmatically with PerformanceObserver const observer = new PerformanceObserver((list) => { for (const entry of list.getEntries()) { if (entry.duration > 50) { console.warn(`Long task detected: ${entry.duration}ms`, entry); } } }); observer.observe({ type: 'longtask', buffered: true }); Performance Budgets & CI Gates Performance budgets enforce thresholds in CI. Common budgets: bundle size ( Lighthouse score (>90), LCP ( bundlesize or Lighthouse CI to fail builds that exceed budgets. A staff engineer sets budgets based on field data percentiles, not arbitrary numbers. JSON // Example: bundlesize configuration (bundlesize.json) { "files": [ { "path": "./dist/main.js", "maxSize": "200 kB" }, { "path": "./dist/vendor.js", "maxSize": "100 kB" } ] } JavaScript // Example: Lighthouse CI configuration (lighthouserc.js) module.exports = { ci: { collect: { url: ['https://example.com'], numberOfRuns: 3 }, assert: { assertions: { 'largest-contentful-paint': ['error', { maxNumericValue: 2500 }], 'cumulative-layout-shift': ['error', { maxNumericValue: 0.1 }], 'interaction-to-next-paint': ['error', { maxNumericValue: 200 }] } }, upload: { target: 'temporary-public-storage' } } }; The Measure → Optimize → Verify Loop This is the core discipline: measure the current state (lab + field), optimize one bottleneck at a time, then verify the improvement with the same metrics. Never skip verification — an optimization that doesn't move the needle is wasted effort. Use A/B testing or feature flags to isolate changes. Avoid Premature Optimization Optimizing before measuring is the #1 performance mistake. A junior engineer might preload every image or inline all CSS, bloating the page. A staff engineer measures first, finds the real bottleneck (e.g., a 300ms server response), and optimizes that. Premature optimization adds complexity without guaranteed benefit. User-Centric Metrics vs Vanity Metrics Vanity metrics like DOMContentLoaded or total page weight don't correlate with user experience. User-centric metrics like LCP , INP , and CLS measure what users actually perceive. A staff engineer ignores vanity metrics and focuses on Core Web Vitals and custom metrics that reflect user tasks (e.g., time to first interaction). Your team's Lighthouse score is 95, but field data shows LCP is 3.2s at p75. What should you do? Optimize the hero image because Lighthouse says it's slow Ignore field data since Lighthouse is the standard Profile the main thread in DevTools to find the real bottleneck, then optimize based on field data Reduce bundle size to improve Lighthouse score further Lighthouse runs on a fast machine; field data reflects real users. The gap indicates a bottleneck (e.g., slow server or third-party scripts) that Lighthouse doesn't catch. Profile the main thread to find the cause, then optimize based on field data percentiles. What is the threshold for a long task? 50ms — tasks longer than this block the main thread and degrade INP. What is the difference between lab and field data? Lab data is synthetic and controlled; field data is from real users and captures variability. What is the measure → optimize → verify loop? Measure current performance, optimize one bottleneck, then verify the improvement with the same metrics. What is a vanity metric? A metric that doesn't correlate with user experience, e.g., DOMContentLoaded or total page weight. What is a performance budget? A limit on metrics (e.g., bundle size <200kB, LCP <2.5s) enforced in CI to prevent regressions.
